content.text:
I've gone through the PDF and all of your design doc, including the diagram and your three open comments, and checked this machine. Most of the design carries straight over. A few things need your input before I start, and a few I'll decide myself unless you object.

**Things I found that the design doesn't account for:**
1. **Your desktop is KDE Plasma 6.6 on Wayland, not GNOME.** The design assumes GNOME/AT-SPI for tracking which app is focused. I'll use a small KWin script that reports window activation and title changes over D-Bus to `brain run`. Reading keystrokes from evdev works as designed, and you're already in the `input` group.
2. **The design contradicts itself on `query text`.** The CLI section says it returns the raw keystroke stream with no backspace applied. But the Known limitations section and Stage 3 both describe a reconstructed point-in-time text. The PDF says *"returns current text, or its text at time T"*, and its example output is clean document text. As designed, it risks failing the spec.
3. **The VS Code tier 2 plan rests on an assumption that isn't true.** VS Code's window title shows only the file name and folder, not the full path, unless you set `window.title` to `${activeEditorLong}`. Also, Xvfb isn't installed, and a warm Electron instance is heavy next to the ≤1% CPU / ≤32 MB budget, even in a separate cgroup.
4. **Some system packages are missing.** Please run: `! sudo apt install -y libxkbcommon-dev xvfb sqlite3`. SQLite with FTS5 will be bundled into the binary; the `sqlite3` CLI is only for inspecting the database.
5. **`/dev/uinput` is root-only**, so automated tests can't type into the real system. I'll make the event source pluggable so most tests replay recorded event streams. For the full end-to-end performance test I'll need either sudo once or a udev rule, and I'll ask when I get there.
6. **The `ai-logs/` deliverable needs your design conversation.** I can't reach the claude.ai chat that produced the design doc, so please export it and drop it into this folder at some point. I'll copy this session's transcripts in myself.

**What I'll decide unless you say otherwise:**
- **Mouse clicks:** I'll log them as events and treat the cursor position as unknown afterwards. Tier 0 will snap the cursor to the end of the text and the README will document this.
- **Paste:** I'll fetch the clipboard text from Klipper over D-Bus when Ctrl+V or Shift+Insert is pressed, on a background thread so typing isn't slowed.
- **Sessions:** each (app, window) keeps a running text buffer across sessions. A session's stored text is that buffer when the session closes. This is what makes "deleted in a later session but still findable in the earlier one" work.
- **Your open doc comments:**
  - Idle timeout: 30 s.
  - Chrome companion extension: not built.
  - VS Code file changed since the session started: flag it and fall back to tier 0.
- **Time formats for `--at`, `--from` and `--to`:** RFC3339, plus local `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]`.

input.prompt:
You are drafting PLAN.md for a home assignment. Write ONLY the file /home/juan/Documents/shadow-assistant/PLAN.md (do not touch any other file; another engineer is writing the Rust code in src/ concurrently — do not read, build, or modify src/ or Cargo.toml).

## The assignment (summary of the PDF at /home/juan/Documents/shadow-assistant/Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf — you may read it with `pdftotext -layout`)
Build one Rust binary `brain` — a "shadow assistant / second brain" that runs on the user's computer:
- `brain run`: captures what the user types (each keystroke: time, app, key, modifiers) and focus changes between apps/contexts, works out what they actually wrote, and stores it.
- `brain query search "<words>" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--limit N]` (all words, case-insensitive, must appear in the same session; a word typed and deleted within the same session doesn't count; a word that existed at the end of a session stays findable in that session even if deleted later) and `brain query text --app A [--at T]`. Both print JSON and work while `run` is writing.
- Hard requirements: no input lag, ≤1% average CPU while typing, ≤32 MB memory, keeps working after sleep/wake; kill -9 at any moment + restart causes no corruption; live queries always see a consistent state; history via `--at`.
- PLAN.md must contain Research and Architecture Design: (1) how you collect keystrokes and application data — COMPARE ALL AVAILABLE APPROACHES; (2) how you ingest the data; (3) how you define sessions; (4) how you store and index the data.
- Evaluation: architecture & code quality, thoughtfulness about edge cases and trade-offs.

## Target platform (this machine — verified)
Ubuntu 26.04, KDE Plasma 6.6 on **Wayland** (kwin_wayland 6.6), systemd 259/logind, user in the `input` group (so /dev/input/event* is readable), /dev/uinput root-only. Keyboard layout `us`, pc105.

## Decided architecture (from the owner's design doc + confirmed decisions — PLAN.md must match these exactly)
- **Capture (hot path)**: read raw key events from evdev (`/dev/input/event*`, all devices with keyboard capability; hotplug via inotify on /dev/input; mouse/touchpad button presses recorded as `click` events because they move the text cursor). Resolve each key to a character at capture time with libxkbcommon using the live keymap (layout read from KDE's kxkbrc, default us) and a single global modifier state, mirroring what the compositor does. Key auto-repeat is re-synthesized using the compositor's repeat delay/rate (KDE kcminputrc, defaults 600 ms / 25 Hz) rather than the kernel's own repeat timing, so the log matches what apps actually received. Append one JSON line per event to an append-only JSONL log, `write()` per event (so a kill -9 loses nothing already captured — page cache survives process death) and batched `fdatasync` (only matters for power loss). On startup, a torn trailing line (no newline) left by kill -9 is truncated. A lock file (flock) prevents two `run`s on one data dir.
- Event format, e.g. `{"ts":"2026-11-08T14:03:22.118Z","app":"code","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"]}` and `{"ts":"…","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"focus","window":"~/src : bash — Konsole"}`. Printable keys are the character; others are names (Enter, Backspace, Left, …). Ctrl+A is key "a" mods ["ctrl"].
- **Focus/app tracking on KDE Wayland**: Wayland deliberately gives clients no global "active window" API, so a KWin script (JavaScript, loaded into the compositor over D-Bus via org.kde.KWin /Scripting loadScript) subscribes to `workspace.windowActivated` and each window's `captionChanged`, and calls `callDBus` into a small D-Bus service that `brain run` exposes on the session bus (zbus). App id = window's desktopFileName (e.g. `code`, `google-chrome`, `org.kde.konsole`), falling back to resourceClass. Works on KWin X11 too. GNOME is out of scope (would need a Shell extension — mention as the equivalent). Screen lock (org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver ActiveChanged) pauses capture so the lock-screen password isn't recorded under the previous app. Sleep/wake: subscribe to systemd-logind `PrepareForSleep`; on resume, reopen input devices and re-register the KWin script.
- **Ingest (cold path, same process, separate thread)**: tails the JSONL log from a byte offset persisted in SQLite (`ingest_state.log_offset`); advances the offset in the SAME transaction as the derived data it writes, so offset and data never drift across a crash; ignores incomplete trailing lines. Writes `log_checkpoints(app, ts, byte_offset)` every few seconds per app so `query text` can seek into the log.
- **Storage**: JSONL log = ground truth; SQLite in WAL mode = derived, rebuildable index (sessions table, FTS5 `sessions_fts` external-content table with `porter unicode61` tokenizer kept in sync by triggers, ingest_state, log_checkpoints). WAL: one writer (ingest) never blocks readers; each `query` reads a consistent snapshot. Raw keystrokes are NOT duplicated into SQLite.
- **Sessions**: keyed by (app, window/context). Close after 30 s with no keystrokes in that context, or immediately on a commit key (Enter) in single-line contexts (terminal prompts, chat compose boxes, browser address bar — via a small explicit app-class table). Focus loss alone never ends a session; returning to the same context within 30 s of its own last keystroke resumes it. Each (app, window) keeps a running text buffer across sessions; a session's stored text is the buffer state when it closes — so a word deleted in a later session is still findable in the earlier one, while a word typed and deleted within one session never appears.
- **Reconstruction (tiers)**: Tier 0 generic buffer replay (virtual cursor/selection: printable chars, Backspace, Delete, arrows, Home/End, Ctrl+Backspace/Ctrl+arrows word ops, Ctrl+A select-all, paste using clipboard text fetched from KDE Klipper over D-Bus on Ctrl+V/Shift+Insert; after a mouse click cursor position is unknown → snap to end, documented limitation). Tier 1 static per-app rules on top (e.g. readline keys in terminals: Ctrl+U/Ctrl+W/Ctrl+A/Ctrl+E). Tier 2 real-app replay for VS Code only and OPT-IN via `brain run --vscode-replay`: replay the session keystrokes over the Chrome DevTools Protocol into a warm, hidden VS Code instance on Xvfb (network-isolated, resource-capped via systemd-run --scope cgroup, serialized, timeout → fallback to tier 0), with a snapshot of the file taken at session start; requires the user to set VS Code `window.title` to include `${activeEditorLong}` so the file path is known. Chrome and terminal stay tier 0/1 (sandboxed-replay designs for both are future work).
- **query search**: FTS5 over closed sessions' reconstructed text + a just-in-time tier-0 reconstruction of currently open sessions; returns session_id, app, started_at, ended_at, snippet.
- **query text**: returns the RAW decoded keystroke stream for the app (exactly the characters captured in order, no backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 minutes; `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T; `--from/--to` explicit. Output `{"app":…,"at":…,"text":…}`. This is a deliberate decision distinct from search's edit-aware text — note it as a decision and the trade-off (the PDF's wording could be read as reconstructed text).
- CLI: both commands take `--data-dir <dir>` (default ./brain-data), exit non-zero with a stderr message on error. Times accept RFC3339 or local `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]`.

## What to write
A well-structured, technically precise PLAN.md (markdown, roughly 400–700 lines is fine) with:
1. Summary + architecture diagram (ASCII or mermaid) of capture → log → ingest → SQLite/FTS → query.
2. **Research: collecting keystrokes and application data — compare ALL realistic approaches on Linux**, in a comparison table plus prose, judged on: works under Wayland?, latency/CPU cost, permissions needed, what it can see (raw keycodes vs resolved chars vs actual text), fidelity of the resulting text, robustness (sleep/wake, hotplug), invasiveness/security. Cover at least: evdev /dev/input reading; libinput as a library (on the same devices); X11 XRecord / XInput2 raw events (and why they don't see native Wayland clients — only XWayland); a uinput/evdev grab-and-forward proxy (EVIOCGRAB) — and why grabbing adds latency/risk; kernel module / eBPF keyboard hooks; AT-SPI accessibility bus (text-changed events, reads actual widget text but app coverage is uneven — GTK/Qt good, Electron/Chrome need flags, terminals poor); input method framework (IBus/Fcitx5 addon) — sees committed text but only in IM-aware clients; compositor-level hooks (KWin effect/plugin, or patching); LD_PRELOAD / toolkit hooks; per-app extensions (browser extension, VS Code extension) — most accurate but per-app. Then the same for **application/focus data**: KWin scripting + D-Bus (chosen), `kdotool`, wlr-foreign-toplevel-management (not on KWin for this purpose / KDE has its own plasma-window-management protocol restricted to privileged clients), X11 _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW (XWayland-only on Wayland), AT-SPI focus events, GNOME Shell extension (for GNOME). Explain the decision and its trade-offs honestly (e.g. evdev sees keys not text; needs input group = can read all keyboards, a real security consideration; resolution must mirror the compositor's keymap; IME/compose/dead keys not handled).
3. Ingestion: the log/offset/transaction design, torn-line handling, crash-recovery walk-through for kill -9 at every interesting point (mid-write of a line, between write and fdatasync, mid SQLite transaction, between session close and FTS update), back-pressure, why a separate thread in the same process.
4. Sessions: definition, rationale, state machine, edge cases (rapid alt-tab, title changes like Chrome tab switches or unsaved-marker "●" in editors — normalize titles by stripping such markers, terminal Enter, idle across sleep, clock changes/NTP jumps, run restart while sessions open — open sessions are rebuilt from the log on restart).
5. Storage & indexing: schema (sessions, sessions_fts external content + triggers, ingest_state, log_checkpoints), why SQLite+WAL+FTS5 (vs tantivy, vs custom inverted index, vs plain files), tokenizer choice and implications (porter stemming makes "migrations" match "migration"; prefix not supported by default), how `--at` and checkpoints work, consistency for concurrent readers, size growth / retention.
6. Query semantics for search and text as above, with JSON shapes.
7. Resource budget strategy (how ≤1% CPU / ≤32 MB is met: no async runtime, epoll loop, small SQLite cache, write-per-event cost estimate at ~10 keystrokes/s) and how it is verified.
8. Security & privacy considerations (passwords, lock screen pause, data dir permissions 0700, clipboard capture).
9. Testing strategy (pluggable event source so tests replay recorded streams; kill -9 crash test; concurrent query consistency test; perf harness; sleep/wake simulation).
10. Risks / known limitations / future work.

Be accurate — if unsure about a specific API detail, describe it at the level you're sure of rather than inventing specifics. No marketing tone. When done, reply with a short summary of the file's structure (under 150 words).

Each (app, window) keeps a running text buffer across sessions; a session's stored text is the buffer state when it closes — so a word deleted in a later session is still findable in the earlier one, while a word typed and deleted within one session never appears.
- **Reconstruction (tiers)**: Tier 0 generic buffer replay (virtual cursor/selection: printable chars, Backspace, Delete, arrows, Home/End, Ctrl+Backspace/Ctrl+arrows word ops, Ctrl+A select-all, paste using clipboard text fetched from KDE Klipper over D-Bus on Ctrl+V/Shift+Insert; after a mouse click cursor position is unknown → snap to end, documented limitation). Tier 1 static per-app rules on top (e.g. readline keys in terminals: Ctrl+U/Ctrl+W/Ctrl+A/Ctrl+E). Tier 2 real-app replay for VS Code only and OPT-IN via `brain run --vscode-replay`: replay the session keystrokes over the Chrome DevTools Protocol into a warm, hidden VS Code instance on Xvfb (network-isolated, resource-capped via systemd-run --scope cgroup, serialized, timeout → fallback to tier 0), with a snapshot of the file taken at session start; requires the user to set VS Code `window.title` to include `${activeEditorLong}` so the file path is known. Chrome and terminal stay tier 0/1 (sandboxed-replay designs for both are future work).
- **query search**: FTS5 over closed sessions' reconstructed text + a just-in-time tier-0 reconstruction of currently open sessions; returns session_id, app, started_at, ended_at, snippet.
- **query text**: returns the RAW decoded keystroke stream for the app (exactly the characters captured in order, no backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 minutes; `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T; `--from/--to` explicit. Output `{"app":…,"at":…,"text":…}`. This is a deliberate decision distinct from search's edit-aware text — note it as a decision and the trade-off (the PDF's wording could be read as reconstructed text).
- CLI: both commands take `--data-dir <dir>` (default ./brain-data), exit non-zero with a stderr message on error. Times accept RFC3339 or local `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS]`.

## What to write
A well-structured, technically precise PLAN.md (markdown, roughly 400–700 lines is fine) with:
1. Summary + architecture diagram (ASCII or mermaid) of capture → log → ingest → SQLite/FTS → query.
2. **Research: collecting keystrokes and application data — compare ALL realistic approaches on Linux**, in a comparison table plus prose, judged on: works under Wayland?, latency/CPU cost, permissions needed, what it can see (raw keycodes vs resolved chars vs actual text), fidelity of the resulting text, robustness (sleep/wake, hotplug), invasiveness/security. Cover at least: evdev /dev/input reading; libinput as a library (on the same devices); X11 XRecord / XInput2 raw events (and why they don't see native Wayland clients — only XWayland); a uinput/evdev grab-and-forward proxy (EVIOCGRAB) — and why grabbing adds latency/risk; kernel module / eBPF keyboard hooks; AT-SPI accessibility bus (text-changed events, reads actual widget text but app coverage is uneven — GTK/Qt good, Electron/Chrome need flags, terminals poor); input method framework (IBus/Fcitx5 addon) — sees committed text but only in IM-aware clients; compositor-level hooks (KWin effect/plugin, or patching); LD_PRELOAD / toolkit hooks; per-app extensions (browser extension, VS Code extension) — most accurate but per-app. Then the same for **application/focus data**: KWin scripting + D-Bus (chosen), `kdotool`, wlr-foreign-toplevel-management (not on KWin for this purpose / KDE has its own plasma-window-management protocol restricted to privileged clients), X11 _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW (XWayland-only on Wayland), AT-SPI focus events, GNOME Shell extension (for GNOME). Explain the decision and its trade-offs honestly (e.g. evdev sees keys not text; needs input group = can read all keyboards, a real security consideration; resolution must mirror the compositor's keymap; IME/compose/dead keys not handled).
3. Ingestion: the log/offset/transaction design, torn-line handling, crash-recovery walk-through for kill -9 at every interesting point (mid-write of a line, between write and fdatasync, mid SQLite transaction, between session close and FTS update), back-pressure, why a separate thread in the same process.
4. Sessions: definition, rationale, state machine, edge cases (rapid alt-tab, title changes like Chrome tab switches or unsaved-marker "●" in editors — normalize titles by stripping such markers, terminal Enter, idle across sleep, clock changes/NTP jumps, run restart while sessions open — open sessions are rebuilt from the log on restart).
5. Storage & indexing: schema (sessions, sessions_fts external content + triggers, ingest_state, log_checkpoints), why SQLite+WAL+FTS5 (vs tantivy, vs custom inverted index, vs plain files), tokenizer choice and implications (porter stemming makes "migrations" match "migration"; prefix not supported by default), how `--at` and checkpoints work, consistency for concurrent readers, size growth / retention.
6. Query semantics for search and text as above, with JSON shapes.
7. Resource budget strategy (how ≤1% CPU / ≤32 MB is met: no async runtime, epoll loop, small SQLite cache, write-per-event cost estimate at ~10 keystrokes/s) and how it is verified.
8. Security & privacy considerations (passwords, lock screen pause, data dir permissions 0700, clipboard capture).
9. Testing strategy (pluggable event source so tests replay recorded streams; kill -9 crash test; concurrent query consistency test; perf harness; sleep/wake simulation).
10. Risks / known limitations / future work.

Be accurate — if unsure about a specific API detail, describe it at the level you're sure of rather than inventing specifics. No marketing tone. When done, reply with a short summary of the file's structure (under 150 words).

# CLAUDE.md — instructions for coding agents working on `brain`

`brain` is a Rust CLI for the Endpoint "Shadow Assistant" home assignment
(`Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf`, not committed). One binary, two commands:
`brain run` captures keystrokes + focus and stores them; `brain query`
(`search`, `text`) answers questions while `run` keeps going.

Design doc (source of truth for architecture):
https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. `/dev/uinput` is
root-only on the dev machine: tests must not depend on it. Use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline without
hardware.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout.

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` returns the **raw decoded keystroke stream** (no
  backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, window); close after 30 s idle in that context or
  on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone never closes a session.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0.
- Work proceeds in 4 stages (capture, query, reconstruction, E2E tests).
  After each stage: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and
  wait for explicit approval** before the next stage.

## Code map

```
src/main.rs              CLI (clap), error → stderr + exit 1
src/capture/mod.rs       `run` orchestration: sources, ingest thread, signals
src/capture/input.rs     poll loop over evdev devices, hotplug, EVIOCSMASK
src/capture/keys.rs      pure key processing: xkb resolution + repeat synthesis
src/capture/xkb.rs       libxkbcommon FFI wrapper
src/capture/recorder.rs  stamps focus, appends to log, clipboard on paste, lock pause
src/capture/desktop.rs   D-Bus: KWin focus script, Klipper, lock, sleep, layouts
src/capture/synthetic.rs synthetic input source for tests/benchmarks
src/eventlog.rs          append-only JSONL log: torn-tail repair, line reader
src/store.rs             SQLite schema (WAL, FTS5), migrations, helpers
src/ingest.rs            log → SQLite, offset advanced in the same transaction
src/event.rs, timefmt.rs event format, timestamp parsing/formatting
tests/                   integration tests that drive the real binary
```

## Working rules

- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (zero warnings) and `cargo test`
  before every commit. Run `cargo test --release --test crash_safety` when
  touching the log, ingest or store.
- Keep the hot path (input thread) free of allocation-heavy work, blocking
  I/O other than the single log `write(2)`, and SQLite.
- The log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived and rebuildable. Never put
  data only in SQLite.
- Commit messages per https://cbea.ms/git-commit/ (imperative subject
  ≤ 50 chars, blank line, body wrapped at 72 explaining what and why).
  Commit at meaningful checkpoints.
- Prefer verifying behaviour by running the binary over reasoning about it;
  report exactly what was tested and what was not.

cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# brain — a shadow assistant for Linux

`brain` runs on your computer, follows what you type in each application and
lets you search it later.

```
brain run                      # capture keystrokes + focus changes, store them
brain query search "<words>"   # (stage 2) full-text search over writing sessions
brain query text --app A       # (stage 2) the raw typed stream of an app
```

> **Status: stage 1 of 4 (capture).** `brain run` captures and stores;
> `brain query` is not implemented yet.

## Supported OS

Ubuntu (tested on 26.04) with **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Key capture
works on any Linux. Focus tracking needs KWin (Wayland or X11). On other
desktops, keys are recorded under the app `unknown`.

## Build

```sh
# Rust toolchain (https://rustup.rs), then:
cargo build --release
# binary: target/release/brain
```

SQLite is bundled. libxkbcommon is loaded from the runtime library
`libxkbcommon.so.0` that every Wayland desktop ships, so no `-dev`
packages are needed.

## Permissions

`brain` reads keyboards directly from `/dev/input/event*` (read-only,
never grabbed, so it cannot add input lag). Your user must be in the `input`
group:

```sh
sudo usermod -aG input "$USER"   # then log out and back in
```

Note that the `input` group can read every input device. That is the price of
display-server-independent capture (see PLAN.md for the alternatives).

## Run

```sh
target/release/brain run --data-dir ~/brain-data
```

`run` stops cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. A `kill -9` is also safe. The next
start repairs a torn last line, if there is one, and resumes ingest exactly
where it stopped.

Data directory (mode 0700):

| File           | What                                                   |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `events.jsonl` | append-only capture log, the ground truth              |
| `brain.db`     | SQLite (WAL) index derived from the log                |
| `run.lock`     | held by the running `brain run` (one per data dir)     |
| `kwin/`        | generated KWin focus-tracking script                   |

Example log lines:

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:01.112Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"focus","window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:02.348Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"],"window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
```

## Tests

```sh
cargo test                                   # unit + integration tests
cargo test --release --test crash_safety     # 25 random kill -9s under load
```
EOF

# brain — a shadow assistant for Linux

`brain` runs on your computer, follows what you type in each application and
lets you search it later.

```
brain run                      # capture keystrokes + focus changes, store them
brain query search "<words>"   # (stage 2) full-text search over writing sessions
brain query text --app A       # (stage 2) the raw typed stream of an app
```

> **Status: stage 1 of 4 (capture).** `brain run` captures and stores;
> `brain query` is not implemented yet.

## Supported OS

Ubuntu (tested on 26.04) with **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Key capture
works on any Linux. Focus tracking needs KWin (Wayland or X11). On other
desktops, keys are recorded under the app `unknown`.

## Build

```sh
# Rust toolchain (https://rustup.rs), then:
cargo build --release
# binary: target/release/brain
```

SQLite is bundled. libxkbcommon is loaded from the runtime library
`libxkbcommon.so.0` that every Wayland desktop ships, so no `-dev`
packages are needed.

## Permissions

`brain` reads keyboards directly from `/dev/input/event*` (read-only,
never grabbed, so it cannot add input lag). Your user must be in the `input`
group:

```sh
sudo usermod -aG input "$USER"   # then log out and back in
```

Note that the `input` group can read every input device. That is the price of
display-server-independent capture (see PLAN.md for the alternatives).

```sh
target/release/brain run --data-dir ~/brain-data
```

`run` stops cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. A `kill -9` is also safe. The next
start repairs a torn last line, if there is one, and resumes ingest exactly
where it stopped.

| File           | What                                                   |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `events.jsonl` | append-only capture log, the ground truth              |
| `brain.db`     | SQLite (WAL) index derived from the log                |
| `run.lock`     | held by the running `brain run` (one per data dir)     |
| `kwin/`        | generated KWin focus-tracking script                   |

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:01.112Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"focus","window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:02.348Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"],"window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
```

## Tests

```sh
cargo test                                   # unit + integration tests
cargo test --release --test crash_safety     # 25 random kill -9s under load
```

content.text:
I've built, tested and pushed Stage 1 (capture) to https://github.com/ChenOhana/shadow-assistant (private). Your screen was locked the whole time, so I could not watch real typing from your keyboard. That is the main thing left for you to check before I start Stage 2.

**What Stage 1 does**
- **Keys:** `brain run` reads your keyboards directly from `/dev/input`. Each key is turned into the character the app actually received, using your real layouts (US and Hebrew, with Alt+Shift switching) and KDE's key-repeat timing. Every keystroke is written as one line to an append-only log, `events.jsonl`, with the app and window title. The format matches the PDF's example, plus a `window` field.
- **App and window:** a small KWin script tells `brain` which app and window are focused, including window-title changes such as switching browser tabs.
- **Clipboard and screen lock:** on Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Shift+V or Shift+Insert it records the clipboard text from Klipper. It pauses while the screen is locked, so your unlock password is never recorded.
- **Sleep/wake and hotplug:** keyboards are re-opened after waking from sleep, and newly plugged keyboards are picked up.
- **SQLite:** a background thread copies the log into SQLite. Per the design, keystrokes aren't duplicated into the database; for now it holds only the ingest position and time markers that let queries jump into the log.

34	        'A'..='Z' => (LETTERS[(c as u8 - b'A') as usize], true),
35	        '1'..='9' => (2 + (c as u8 - b'1') as u16, false),
36	        '0' => (11, false),
37	        ' ' => (57, false),
38	        '\n' => (28, false),
39	        '.' => (52, false),
40	        ',' => (51, false),
41	        ';' => (39, false),
42	        ':' => (39, true),
43	        '?' => (53, true),
44	        '-' => (12, false),
45	        '\'' => (40, false),
46	        _ => return None,
47	    })
48	}

50	/// Types the corpus until `stop` is set. Every 50th word gets a typo that is
51	/// immediately corrected with Backspace, to exercise editing keys.
52	pub fn run(mut keys: KeyProcessor, recorder: Arc<Recorder>, rate_hz: f64, stop: Arc<AtomicBool>) {
53	    recorder.set_focus(SYNTHETIC_APP, SYNTHETIC_WINDOW);
54	    let period = Duration::from_secs_f64(1.0 / rate_hz.max(0.1));
55	    let start = Instant::now();
56	    let mut presses: u64 = 0;
57	    let mut words: u64 = 0;
58	    let mut emit = |k: KeyOut| recorder.key(k.ts, k.key, k.mods, k.repeat);
59	    'outer: loop {
60	        for c in CORPUS.chars() {
61	            let Some((code, shift)) = us_keycode(c) else {
62	                continue;
63	            };
64	            let mut strokes: Vec<(u16, bool)> = vec![(code, shift)];
65	            if c == ' ' {
66	                words += 1;
67	                if words.is_multiple_of(50) {
68	                    strokes.insert(0, (us_keycode('x').unwrap().0, false));
69	                    strokes.insert(1, (KEY_BACKSPACE, false));
70	                }
71	            }
72	            for (code, shift) in strokes {
73	                if stop.load(Ordering::Relaxed) {
74	                    break 'outer;
75	                }
76	                // Pace against the start time so the long-run rate is exact.
77	                presses += 1;
78	                let due = start + period.mul_f64(presses as f64);
79	                if let Some(wait) = due.checked_duration_since(Instant::now()) {
80	                    std::thread::sleep(wait);
81	                }
82	                let ts = now_ms();
83	                if shift {
84	                    keys.key(0, KEY_LEFTSHIFT, 1, ts, &mut emit);
85	                }
86	                keys.key(0, code, 1, ts, &mut emit);
87	                keys.key(0, code, 0, ts, &mut emit);
88	                if shift {
89	                    keys.key(0, KEY_LEFTSHIFT, 0, ts, &mut emit);
90	                }

2	//!
3	//! WAL mode gives the concurrency model `brain` needs. The single writer (the
4	//! ingest thread inside `brain run`) never blocks readers. Each `brain query`

7	//! derives from those log bytes, so after a crash the index and the offset
8	//! always agree.

11	//! may drop the last few committed transactions, and the log is fsync'd

102	    let version: i64 = conn.query_row("PRAGMA user_version", [], |r| r.get(0))?;
103	    if version != SCHEMA_VERSION {
104	        bail!(
105	            "database {} has schema version {version}, this brain expects {SCHEMA_VERSION} \
106	             (restart `brain run` to migrate it)",
107	            path.display()
108	        );
109	    }
110	    Ok(conn)
111	}
112	
113	fn migrate(conn: &Connection) -> Result<()> {
114	    let version: i64 = conn.query_row("PRAGMA user_version", [], |r| r.get(0))?;
115	    match version {
116	        0 => {
117	            let tx = conn.unchecked_transaction()?;
118	            tx.execute_batch(SCHEMA_V1)?;
119	            tx.pragma_update(None, "user_version", SCHEMA_VERSION)?;
120	            tx.commit()?;
121	            Ok(())
122	        }
123	        SCHEMA_VERSION => Ok(()),
124	        v => bail!("database schema version {v} is newer than this brain ({SCHEMA_VERSION})"),
125	    }
126	}
127	
128	pub fn ingest_offset(conn: &Connection) -> Result<u64> {
129	    let off: i64 = conn.query_row(
130	        "SELECT log_offset FROM ingest_state WHERE id = 1",
131	        [],
132	        |r| r.get(0),
133	    )?;
134	    Ok(off as u64)
135	}
136	
137	pub fn set_ingest_offset(conn: &Connection, offset: u64) -> Result<()> {
138	    conn.execute(
139	        "UPDATE ingest_state SET log_offset = ?1 WHERE id = 1",
140	        [offset as i64],
141	    )?;
142	    Ok(())
143	}
144	
145	pub fn insert_checkpoint(conn: &Connection, app: &str, ts: &str, offset: u64) -> Result<()> {
146	    conn.prepare_cached(
147	        "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO log_checkpoints (app, ts, byte_offset) VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3)",
148	    )?
149	    .execute(rusqlite::params![app, ts, offset as i64])?;
150	    Ok(())
151	}
152	
153	/// Latest checkpoint timestamp per app, used to resume checkpoint spacing after a restart.
154	pub fn latest_checkpoints(conn: &Connection) -> Result<Vec<(String, String)>> {
155	    let mut stmt = conn.prepare("SELECT app, MAX(ts) FROM log_checkpoints GROUP BY app")?;
156	    let rows = stmt
157	        .query_map([], |r| Ok((r.get::<_, String>(0)?, r.get::<_, String>(1)?)))?
158	        .collect::<rusqlite::Result<Vec<_>>>()?;
159	    Ok(rows)
160	}
161	
162	/// Byte offset of the latest global checkpoint at or before `ts`, or 0.
163	pub fn seek_offset_before(conn: &Connection, ts: &str) -> Result<u64> {
164	    let off: Option<i64> = conn
165	        .query_row(
166	            "SELECT byte_offset FROM log_checkpoints WHERE app = ?1 AND ts <= ?2
167	             ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1",
168	            rusqlite::params![GLOBAL_CHECKPOINT_APP, ts],
169	            |r| r.get(0),
170	        )
171	        .optional()?;
172	    Ok(off.unwrap_or(0) as u64)
173	}

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## Quick Reference

| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Merge PDFs | pypdf | `writer.add_page(page)` |
| Split PDFs | pypdf | One page per file |
| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
| Create PDFs | reportlab | Canvas or Platypus |
| Command line merge | qpdf | `qpdf --empty --pages ...` |
| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
| Fill PDF forms | pdf-lib or pypdf (see FORMS.md) | See FORMS.md |

## Next Steps

- For advanced pypdfium2 usage, see REFERENCE.md
- For JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib), see REFERENCE.md
- If you need to fill out a PDF form, follow the instructions in FORMS.md
- For troubleshooting guides, see REFERENCE.md

# CLAUDE.md — instructions for coding agents working on `brain`

`brain` is a Rust CLI for the Endpoint "Shadow Assistant" home assignment
(`Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf`, not committed). One binary, two commands:
`brain run` captures keystrokes + focus and stores them; `brain query`
(`search`, `text`) answers questions while `run` keeps going.

Design doc (source of truth for architecture):
https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. `/dev/uinput` is
root-only on the dev machine: tests must not depend on it. Use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline without
hardware.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout.

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` returns the **raw decoded keystroke stream** (no
  backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, window); close after 30 s idle in that context or
  on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone never closes a session.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0.
- Work proceeds in 4 stages (capture, query, reconstruction, E2E tests).
  After each stage: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and
  wait for explicit approval** before the next stage.

## Code map

```
src/main.rs              CLI (clap), error → stderr + exit 1
src/capture/mod.rs       `run` orchestration: sources, ingest thread, signals
src/capture/input.rs     poll loop over evdev devices, hotplug, EVIOCSMASK
src/capture/keys.rs      pure key processing: xkb resolution + repeat synthesis
src/capture/xkb.rs       libxkbcommon FFI wrapper
src/capture/recorder.rs  stamps focus, appends to log, clipboard on paste, lock pause
src/capture/desktop.rs   D-Bus: KWin focus script, Klipper, lock, sleep, layouts
src/capture/synthetic.rs synthetic input source for tests/benchmarks
src/eventlog.rs          append-only JSONL log: torn-tail repair, line reader
src/store.rs             SQLite schema (WAL, FTS5), migrations, helpers
src/ingest.rs            log → SQLite, offset advanced in the same transaction
src/event.rs, timefmt.rs event format, timestamp parsing/formatting
tests/                   integration tests that drive the real binary
```

## Working rules

- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (zero warnings) and `cargo test`
  before every commit. Run `cargo test --release --test crash_safety` when
  touching the log, ingest or store.
- Keep the hot path (input thread) free of allocation-heavy work, blocking
  I/O other than the single log `write(2)`, and SQLite.
- The log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived and rebuildable. Never put
  data only in SQLite.
- Commit messages per https://cbea.ms/git-commit/ (imperative subject
  ≤ 50 chars, blank line, body wrapped at 72 explaining what and why).
  Commit at meaningful checkpoints.
- Prefer verifying behaviour by running the binary over reasoning about it;
  report exactly what was tested and what was not.
- [brain assignment decisions](brain-assignment-decisions.md) — user-confirmed choices: raw `query text`, stage gates, opt-in VS Code tier 2, private repo; KDE Wayland machine
